stem: Each of the following numbers has a two-digit pattern property. Three share the same property; one does not. Find the odd one out: 121, 169, 196, 225.

per_option_rationale.rationale: 121 = 11^2, a palindrome AND a perfect square. It passes both properties but is not the odd one out because the key property is palindrome nature. 121 reversed is 121 (palindrome).

169 reversed is 961 = 31^2, also a perfect square. However, 169 itself is a palindrome? No, 169 reversed is 961 which is different. The property here is: the number is a perfect square whose digit-reversal is also a perfect square. 169 = 13^2, reversed 961 = 31^2. This holds.
196 = 14^2. Reversed: 691. Is 691 a perfect square? sqrt(691) ~ 26.29, not a perfect square. So 196 fails the property that its reversal is also a perfect square.

225 = 15^2. Reversed: 522. Is 522 a perfect square? sqrt(522) ~ 22.84, not a perfect square. Wait - re-checking the property: 121 reversed = 121 = 11^2 (yes), 169 reversed = 961 = 31^2 (yes), 225 reversed = 522 (not a perfect square). So 225 also fails. The actual property that three share and one does not must be reconsidered. Let us use: palindrome squares. 121 is a palindrome square (11^2). The others are not palindromes. So the property of three is being a perfect square with consecutive integer roots: 11, 12, 13... Wait. Let us use a clear property: digit sum divisible by 9. 1+2+1=4 (no), 1+6+9=16 (no), 1+9+6=16 (no), 2+2+5=9 (yes). That does not work. Using the property: all are perfect squares (true for all four). The distinguishing property must be finer. Key insight: 121=11^2, 169=13^2, 225=15^2 are all squares of ODD numbers. 196=14^2 is the square of an EVEN number. That is the clean property.

explanation: 121 = 11^2, 169 = 13^2, 225 = 15^2 are all squares of odd integers. 196 = 14^2 is the square of an even integer. The property shared by three is: perfect square of an odd number. 196 is the odd one out.

explanation_sections.punchline: Three are squares of odd numbers (11, 13, 15); 196 = 14^2 is the only square of an even number.
explanation_sections.approach: Apply clues most-certain-first: find the square root of each number. sqrt(121)=11 (odd), sqrt(169)=13 (odd), sqrt(196)=14 (even), sqrt(225)=15 (odd). The one with an even square root is the odd one out.
explanation_sections.lesson: After confirming all four share the perfect-square property, test the parity of the square root to find the finer distinguishing rule.
explanation_sections.timing: About 60 seconds. The trap is 196 which, being even, looks similar to 196 in context with other three-digit numbers. The key move is computing each square root.
